claims.text: Premelting and melting in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles are governed by a two-phase coexistence mechanism.
Element-specific diffusion initiates melting from the nanoparticle surface inward.
Fe is preferentially mobile because it has elevated local potential energy.
Cu is preferentially mobile because of its lower melting point.
Melting proceeds without formation of a persistent liquid shell.
The modeled initial particles are random equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu FCC nanoparticles containing 20 at.% of each element.
The initial FCC lattice parameter is 3.52 Å.
Fe has a local potential energy approximately 0.5 eV higher than the other species.
High-displacement atoms are initially confined to approximately two to three surface layers around 900 K.
Initial Fe and Cu mobility gradually propagates from the surface into the nanoparticle core.
Larger Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles have higher melting temperatures than smaller nanoparticles.
Nanoparticle melting temperature follows an inverse-radius relation.
The melting temperature approaches a fitted bulk melting limit of approximately 2184 K as particle size increases.
Early preferential Fe and Cu mobility occurs without significant persistent surface-liquid layers.
Melting occurs without elemental clustering under the specified simulation conditions.
The proposed behavior applies over nanoparticle radii of approximately 5–40 Å under the specified heating protocol.
Changing the interatomic potential, composition, or heating conditions may change the behavior.

contradictions.description: The protocol is described as NVE while also using repeated velocity rescaling during heating. Velocity rescaling changes particle kinetic energy, so the rescaled portions are not strictly microcanonical NVE dynamics unless NVE refers only to the intervals between rescaling operations.
